results.content: > Recent self-supervised methods for image representation learning maximize the agreement between embedding vectors produced by encoders fed with different views of the same image. We introduce VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization), a method that explicitly avoids the collapse problem with two regularizations terms applied to both embeddings separately: (1) a term that maintains the variance of each embedding dimension above a threshold, (2) a term that decorrelates each pair of variables. self-supervised learning method for training embeddings from images (though could probably be applied to other modalities) where the model generates outputs from two transformed version of the input and tries to ensure that the output embeddings are similar (invariance), the individual dimensions of the embeddings vary enough within a batch (variance), and the covariances among the dimensions are minimized (covariance).

results.content: # What Is A Variance Threshold? What Is A Variance Threshold? In this informative video, we will discuss the concept of variance thresholds and their role in data analysis and machine learning. A variance threshold is a technique that helps in identifying and filtering out features that exhibit minimal variation across samples. Understanding how to effectively apply a variance threshold can significantly streamline your data processing and enhance the performance of your models. We'll cover the steps involved in calculating variance, defining a threshold, and removing low-variance features from your dataset. By focusing on features that demonstrate meaningful variation, you can improve the quality of your data and make your models more efficient. Moreover, we will explore practical applications of variance thresholding, including its impact on machine learning performance, computational efficiency, and data interpretation. Whether you're a data scientist, a student, or someone interested in data analysis, this video will provide you with essential knowledge about variance thresholds and their significance in the measurement and data field. What is a variance threshold? In simple terms, it is a technique used in data analysis and machine learning to filter out features that do not vary much across samples. Variance measures how much the values of a feature differ from one another. When a feature has low variance, it means that its values are almost constant. By setting a specific variance threshold, you can identify features whose variance falls below this cutoff. These low variance features are then removed from the data set. First, you calculate the variance of each feature in your data set. After that, you remove features that have variance below this threshold. Finally, you keep the features with variance above the threshold for further analysis or modeling. From a measurement and data perspective, variance thresholding focuses on the statistical property of variance as a measure of data spread. By removing these low variance features, you improve the quality of the data, concentrating on variables that capture meaningful variation. Practical applications of variance thresholding include improving the performance of machine learning models by reducing noise and irrelevant features. In summary, a variance threshold is a straightforward method to filter out features with little variability.

results.title: ICLR Poster VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning
results.content: Skip to yearly menu bar. ## Main Navigation. # VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning. Adrien Bardes · Jean Ponce · Yann LeCun. Keywords: representation learning self-supervised learning computer vision. [Visit Poster at Spot F3 in Virtual World ] [OpenReview]. ### Abstract. Recent self-supervised methods for image representation learning maximize the agreement between embedding vectors produced by encoders fed with different views of the same image. The main challenge is to prevent a collapse in which the encoders produce constant or non-informative vectors. We introduce VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization), a method that explicitly avoids the collapse problem with two regularizations terms applied to both embeddings separately: (1) a term that maintains the variance of each embedding dimension above a threshold, (2) a term that decorrelates each pair of variables. Unlike most other approaches to the same problem, VICReg does not require techniques such as: weight sharing between the branches, batch normalization, feature-wise normalization, output quantization, stop gradient, memory banks, etc., and achieves results on par with the state of the art on several downstream tasks. In addition, we show that our variance regularization term stabilizes the training of other methods and leads to performance improvements. ### Video.
